beats.say: Day one at Cymbal Retail, and the security chief hands you a list.
beats.sub: The security chief hands you a list.

beats.say: Analysts can see every table. Card numbers sit in plain columns. And nobody knows who could copy the data out.
beats.label: The list

beats.say: Your job: lock it down, without slowing anyone down.
Six ideas do it. Let's take them one at a time.
beats.label: Station 1.1 · Security and compliance
beats.head: Six ideas, one at a time

check.prompt: An analyst must run queries, but read only one dataset. Which grant fits?
options: jobUser on the project + dataViewer on that dataset
check.why: jobUser lets the analyst run queries. dataViewer on one dataset limits what the analyst can read.

beats.say: First, IAM. It answers one question: who can do what, on which resource?
Think of an office building. A badge for every door is risky. A badge for one room is safe.
beats.label: Think of a building
beats.head: A badge for one room, not every door

beats.say: Access flows down: from the organization, to folders, to projects, to each resource.
beats.label: Grants inherit downward

beats.say: So a wide grant at the top cannot be undone lower down.
beats.label: Exam trap
beats.text: A wide grant at the top cannot be undone lower down.

beats.say: Basic roles, like Owner and Editor, are almost always the wrong answer.
The safe pattern: the narrowest predefined role, on the smallest resource, given to a group.
beats.label: Least privilege
beats.head: Narrowest role. Smallest resource. A group.

beats.say: For an analyst, that is job user on the project, plus data viewer on one dataset.
beats.label: The analyst pattern
beats.text: jobUser on the project + dataViewer on one dataset

beats.say: Next: what if people should see only part of a table?
Use the coarsest control that works. Usually, that is a separate dataset.
beats.label: The rule
beats.head: Use the coarsest control that works

beats.say: An authorized view shares the results, but hides the source tables.
beats.label: Authorized view
beats.head: Shares results, hides the source

beats.say: A row access policy shows each team only its own rows.
beats.label: Row access policy
beats.head: Each team sees only its own rows

beats.say: A policy tag hides one column, or masks it, like a card number.
beats.label: Policy tag + masking
beats.head: Hide or mask one column

beats.say: The trap is copying data into many filtered tables. Never do that.
beats.label: Exam trap
beats.text: Copying data into many filtered tables

beats.say: Third idea: encryption. Good news: it is always on.
beats.sub: At rest and in transit. Nothing to set up.

beats.say: So the exam never asks if data is encrypted. It asks who holds the key.
beats.label: The real question
beats.head: Who holds the key?

beats.say: By default, Google holds it. With CMEK, you hold it, in Cloud KMS.
beats.label: Who holds the key

beats.say: Must the key stay outside Google? That is Cloud EKM.
beats.label: Key outside Google
beats.head: Cloud EKM

beats.say: If a rule demands hardware keys, add Cloud HSM.
beats.label: Regulation says hardware
beats.head: CMEK + Cloud HSM

beats.say: One more thing. Rotating a key does not re-encrypt old data.
beats.label: Remember
beats.text: Rotating a key does not re-encrypt old data.

beats.say: Fourth: personal data, like card numbers and emails.
Sensitive Data Protection, also called Cloud DLP, finds it for you, across thousands of tables.
beats.label: Sensitive Data Protection · Cloud DLP
beats.head: Finds PII across thousands of tables

beats.say: Then it hides it. And how you hide it is the exam question.
Never need it back? Mask it. Need joins? Hash it. Need the original later? Use deterministic encryption.
beats.label: Pick by what you need later

beats.say: And to keep a sixteen digit card looking like a card, use format-preserving encryption.
beats.label: Keep the shape
beats.text: 16 digits in, 16 digits out: format-preserving encryption

check.prompt: A user with valid access copies a table to a personal project. What stops this?
check.why: IAM says who can act. Only a VPC Service Controls perimeter says where the data may go.

beats.say: Fifth: stopping data from leaving.
IAM alone cannot do it. A valid user can still copy a table to a personal project.
beats.label: The gap
beats.text: A valid user can still copy a table to a personal project.

beats.say: VPC Service Controls draws a wall around your projects. Data cannot cross it, even with valid IAM.
beats.label: VPC Service Controls
beats.head: A wall around your projects

beats.say: Must data stay in one country? Use regional resources, plus the resource locations org policy.
beats.label: Data residency
beats.head: Regional resources + an org policy

beats.say: And remember: a BigQuery dataset's location can never change. You copy it instead.
beats.label: Exam trap
beats.text: A dataset's location can never change.

beats.say: Last idea: how you lay things out.
Give dev, test and prod their own projects. A mistake in dev then stays in dev.
beats.label: Environments
beats.head: One project each: dev, test, prod

beats.say: In BigQuery, the dataset is the security boundary. So: one client, one dataset.
beats.label: Tenants
beats.head: One client, one dataset

beats.say: And before you lock anything down, read the audit logs to see who uses what.
beats.label: First step
beats.head: Read the audit logs first

beats.say: Let's recap, in twenty seconds.
Give the narrowest role, to a group. Use the coarsest control that works. And know who holds the key.
beats.label: Recap · 1 of 2

beats.say: Hide PII by what you need later. Block leaks with VPC Service Controls. And split projects by environment.
beats.label: Recap · 2 of 2
items: Hide PII by what you need later

beats.say: Now scroll down, and prove it at the checkpoint.
beats.sub: Scroll down and pass the checkpoint.
